overview: This file concerns two rare but fatal accidents in Japanese civil aviation between 1931 and 1938, together with later records-management material. A cross-reference and report extract describe the Japan Air Transport Company’s first major accident, a fiery crash in Kyushu that killed three people, while a consular despatch reports an air-mail plane’s loss near the Penghu Islands, the presumed drowning of its pilot and mechanic, the recovery of the aircraft and mail, and plans to add passenger service to the route. The final pages are an administrative change slip and an otherwise unexplained numerical filing table.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Forbes report on Japan Air Transport accident
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file for report no. 261 concerning a Japan Air Transport Company accident that killed three people.
subfiles.summary: This records-control note cross-references report no. 261 from Forbes in Japan, dated June 30, 1931, to file 894.00 P R/43. It identifies the subject as an accident involving a Japan Air Transport Company aircraft in which three persons were killed.

subfiles.title: Extract on the first major Japanese commercial aviation accident
subfiles.about: The extract describes a June 22 crash in Kyushu that killed three people and reviews the Japan Air Transport Company’s previously fatality-free expansion.
subfiles.summary: A Japan Air Transport Company aircraft reportedly caught fire while crossing the mountains of Kyushu and plunged to earth, killing a passenger and two other people. The cause remained unknown. The account calls this the first accident of substantial magnitude in Japanese commercial aviation and notes that the company had carried thousands of passengers without a fatality since assuming the Tokyo–Osaka service in 1929 and extending it through Fukuoka and Korea to Dalian.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese air-mail plane lost near the Penghu Islands
subfiles.about: Warner reports the loss of a Japanese air-mail plane near Penghu, the disappearance of its two crewmen, and the recovery of the aircraft and mail.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports that an air-mail landplane flying from Tainan to Magong developed engine trouble on March 17, 1938, and fell into the sea near Ryobunko on the eastern Penghu coast. A mail boat and destroyer found the aircraft still afloat, but pilot Sonehara and mechanic Horiuchi had disappeared and were presumed drowned after an unsuccessful sea-and-air search. The plane was towed to Magong with its mail intact. Warner adds that passenger service was planned for the route beginning April 1 and characterizes the event as one of the few accidents suffered by the Japanese air-mail service.

subfiles.title: Records change slip for file 894.79653F
subfiles.about: The slip records an administrative change involving F. E. Coville and file 894.79653F.
subfiles.summary: This records-management form bears file number 894.79653F and an entry dated February 6, 1941. It names F. E. Coville, gives the client’s initials as W.N., and includes the remark “tel 42 of 2442,” whose precise meaning is unclear from the OCR.

subfiles.title: Unidentified numerical filing table
subfiles.about: The page contains an unexplained four-column sequence of numbers from 1817 through 1826.
subfiles.summary: This page consists solely of a four-column numerical table in which consecutive values from 1817 to 1826 are repeated in offset rows. It has no visible title, date, names, or narrative explanation, although its position suggests that it may be records-control material associated with the preceding change slip.

interest: The file provides a compact comparison between two uncommon but deadly mishaps during the early development of Japan’s scheduled air network: a 1931 commercial passenger crash and a 1938 colonial air-mail loss. It is especially useful for reconstructing routes linking the Japanese home islands with Korea, Dalian, Taiwan, and Penghu, as well as contemporary rescue procedures and official perceptions of aviation safety. The intact recovery of the mail despite the disappearance of both crewmen is a striking detail, while the cross-reference and later change slip illustrate how the State Department’s decimal files were organized and revised.
